entry.title: LangChain Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Framework Behind Millions of LLM Apps

link.title: LangChain Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Framework Behind Millions of LLM Apps

entry.content:
Every LLM application eventually turns into the same pile of glue. You concatenate prompts, wrap a provider SDK call in retry logic, parse replies with string hacks, feed tool results back into the conversation, and stitch retrieved documents from a vector store such as Qdrant into the context. Then a provider ships a new API, or you add a second model vendor, and the glue multiplies: streaming shapes differ, function-calling formats differ, error taxonomies differ. The interesting part of your application drowns in plumbing.

LangChain’s bet is that this plumbing deserves its own layer, and millions of LLM apps have agreed. The framework reduces the chaos to a short list of abstractions: standardized messages, a BaseChatModel contract, composable Runnables, schema-carrying tools, and, since the 1.0 restructuring, a single factory function named create_agent. Read the source and the mystique evaporates: an “agent” is a compiled LangGraph state machine with a model node, a tools node, and a conditional edge that loops until the model stops requesting tools. That is genuinely all it is — and it turns out to be enough.

This tour reads the master branch of langchain-ai/langchain as it exists after the v1.0 reorganization: framework primitives live in libs/core/langchain_core, the v1 langchain package in libs/langchain_v1, and vendor integrations under libs/partners. Two diagrams anchor the walk — an overview of the main flow and a detail map of the internals — and every symbol cited below was verified in the tree, with line numbers you can click through to GitHub.

Figure 1 — LangChain's main flow: messages enter a chat model, responses come back as messages, and the agent loop wires models and tools into a LangGraph state machine wrapped by middleware.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Input is normalized into messages first: HumanMessage, L9 extends BaseMessage, L93, so every component speaks one data format.
  • BaseChatModel, L325 is the single model contract: invoke (L516) delegates to generate (L1635), which finally calls the abstract _generate (L2252) that providers implement.
  • Replies are messages too: AIMessage, L160 carries content plus tool_calls, the field that drives the entire agent loop.
  • Runnable, L197 gives models, parsers, tools and lambdas one invoke/batch/stream surface; the | operator composes them into a RunnableSequence, L3094.
  • RunnableSequence.invoke, L3449 is the heart of composition: a plain for-loop over steps, opening a child callback run per step and piping each output forward.
  • BaseTool, L433 makes tools Runnables with a schema; run (L1009) validates arguments against args_schema before dispatching to _run (L909).
  • create_agent, L892 builds the loop: a StateGraph, L1239 gets a model node (L1611) and a tools node (L1615), then graph.compile() (L1909) returns the agent.
  • AgentMiddleware, L385 injects before_model (L455), after_model (L479) and wrap_model_call (L503) hooks around the loop without any subclassing.

Figure 2 — The internals: message hierarchy, the generate path down to provider hooks, runnable composition and resilience wrappers, tool validation, and the exact graph wiring inside create_agent.

One Contract for Every Provider

Open libs/core/langchain_core/language_models/chat_models.py and you find the layer that made LangChain famous: BaseChatModel, L325 owns everything except the HTTP call. The public entry point invoke (L516) normalizes input and opens a callback run; generate (L1635) adds batching, cache lookups and usage accounting; only at the bottom does the abstract _generate (L2252) appear — the one method a provider package like langchain-openai must write. Streaming follows the same split: the default stream, L770 implementation uses the provider’s _stream when available and otherwise falls back to chunked generation, so every model “just streams” from the caller’s perspective. Throttling lives in the base class too: a rate_limiter field (L375) is acquired with blocking=True inside generate (L1978) and the streaming paths (L829) before any request leaves the process, which is why swapping providers does not mean rewriting your backoff logic.

Construction is string-driven and lazy. init_chat_model, L197 parses identifiers like openai:gpt-5.5 via _parse_model (L623), infers the provider from name prefixes when you omit it (L547), and imports the integration package on demand. Swapping vendors is a string edit, which is the entire point of the abstraction.

Runnables: Why the Pipe Operator Works

Anything with Runnable, L197 in its ancestry exposes the same surface, so prompt | model | parser is one object you can invoke, stream, batch or save. RunnableSequence.invoke, L3449 iterates self.steps, starting a child callback run per step and feeding each output to the next input. Plain functions join chains through RunnableLambda, L4722, and fan-out maps are handled by RunnableParallel (L3883).

Resilience is composition too. .with_retry() (L2153) wraps any step in RunnableRetry, L50 with exponential backoff, and .with_fallbacks() (L2243) produces a RunnableWithFallbacks, L37 that tries alternates on failure. Parsers close the loop: StrOutputParser, L8 extends BaseOutputParser, L140, itself a Runnable, and JsonOutputParser (L32 in json.py) feeds structured output to your code. Retrieval fits the same shape — a similarity search against FAISS or another index is just another step in the sequence.

Batching shows the engine room. RunnableSequence.batch, L3525 runs step i across all surviving inputs before moving to step i + 1 — true stepwise batching, not a loop of independent chains. Each per-step child run is named seq:step:N (L3587), and a failure map (L3569) tracks inputs that already errored so downstream steps skip them when return_exceptions is set.

The Agent Is a Two-Node Graph

create_agent, L892 is where the “agent” keyword dissolves. Its docstring says it plainly: it “creates an agent graph that calls tools in a loop until a stopping condition is met” (L912). A string model is resolved through init_chat_model (L1048); the factory then builds a StateGraph, L1239 over an AgentState whose core field is the message list, binds tools in _get_bound_model (L1350), and registers exactly two nodes: model_node (L1520, added at L1611) and the tools node (L1615), skipped entirely when you pass no tools. A conditional edge inspects the last AIMessage: if it carries tool_calls, the graph emits Send(‘tools’, …), L2032 — one per call — otherwise the loop ends and graph.compile() (L1909) hands back a runnable graph. Structured output rides the same loop: a response_format argument accepts a Pydantic schema or a ToolStrategy/ProviderStrategy (per the factory docstring, L954), and matching structured tool calls are intercepted before they reach the tools node.

Two details deserve attention. First, the tools node is not reimplemented: LangChain re-exports ToolNode from langgraph.prebuilt through a one-line shim, L4, so execution semantics live in the LangGraph runtime. Second, because the agent is a graph, persistence is native — pass a checkpointer and conversation state survives invocations, a pattern you can back with Postgres for durable, multi-session agents. What reads as “a loop” is literally a small graph with explicit hops: the START edge lands at the entry node (L1743) and after-model middleware edges are wired one hop past the model node (L1857).

Middleware Instead of Subclasses

Version 1 replaced the old executor-style customization with an interceptor list. AgentMiddleware, L385 declares before_model, L455 and after_model, L479, which run around every model call and may rewrite state, plus wrap_model_call, L503, an onion-style wrapper around the request itself, and before_agent/after_agent (L431/L650) bracketing the whole run. The request a wrapper sees is a typed ModelRequest (L88) — messages, model handle and runtime context — so a hook can edit what the model is about to receive without touching the graph. The factory wires each hook into the graph as real nodes and edges — after-model hooks literally become graph hops (L1857).

A standard library of middleware ships alongside: SummarizationMiddleware, L262 compresses history when it outgrows a trigger, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, L397 pauses for approve/edit/reject decisions on risky tools, and ModelFallbackMiddleware (L342) plus ModelRetryMiddleware (L33) add provider-level resilience. Because middleware declares its own state fields, features compose without inheritance — the same philosophy that makes external caches such as Redis easy to bolt onto a running agent.

From Install to Your First Model

The README quickstart is deliberately short. Install with uv add langchain, then:

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")
result = model.invoke("Hello, world!")

On first call, init_chat_model routes to _init_chat_model_helper (L536): the string is split by _parse_model (L623), the provider is matched against the built-in registry (L56) or inferred from the model-name prefix, and _get_chat_model_creator (L153) uses importlib to import the integration package — langchain-openai for the openai key. If that package is missing you get an ImportError naming the exact pip install target (L147), which is the framework’s intended discovery mechanism. Passing a bare model name like claude-... works too via prefix heuristics. To go from chat to agent, hand the same string to create_agent with a tools list; the factory resolves it identically and returns a compiled graph you can invoke, stream or checkpoint.

Honest Limits

  • Indirection has a price. One invoke crosses invoke → generate → _generate → the provider client, and inside an agent those layers sit under a LangGraph execution as well. Stack traces span several frames before you reach your bug.
  • Version churn is real. The 1.0 restructuring split the monorepo: legacy code ships as langchain_classic under libs/langchain, the v1 package lives in libs/langchain_v1, and imports moved with them. Pre-2025 tutorials routinely reference paths that no longer resolve.
  • Quirks are encapsulated, not eliminated. The _generate hook still carries provider-specific kwargs, rate limits and streaming caveats; the standard interface hides differences but does not remove the need to read provider documentation.
  • Overhead for trivial apps. A single one-shot LLM call wrapped in callback managers and runnable metadata buys little; the abstractions pay off only once you compose steps, retry, stream or loop.
  • Docs caveats. The repository README is a landing page: a three-line quickstart and links. Integration-package install guidance first appears inside ImportError messages, and the real documentation lives off-repo at docs.langchain.com.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of LangChain's master branch: chat models, runnables, tools, the create_agent loop and middleware, with two verified architecture diagrams.

entry.title: BadgerDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Pure-Go LSM Key-Value Store

link.title: BadgerDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Pure-Go LSM Key-Value Store

entry.content:
Most storage engines we have toured in this series descend from the same C++ lineage: RocksDB and LevelDB pack keys and values into the same LSM tree and pay for it with compaction write amplification. BadgerDB, maintained by the Dgraph/Hypermode team, makes the opposite bet. It is an embeddable, persistent, pure-Go key-value store — no cgo, no C toolchain — built around the WiscKey paper (FAST ‘16), which separates keys from values so the LSM only ever carries tiny pointers. Badger is the storage engine underneath the Dgraph graph database, and it also powers Jaeger Tracing, so it is battle-tested on data sets the README describes as worth hundreds of terabytes.

Why should AI/ML infrastructure people care? Because Go increasingly hosts the serving side of ML systems: feature stores, agent state, session memory, and embedding caches live inside Go services where an embedded store beats a networked database by removing a hop. Badger’s key-value separation is especially friendly to that workload — large values like embedding vectors or serialized features are appended to an append-only value log, so compaction never rewrites them and reads of big values are fast sequential log reads. The README’s own comparison table highlights “high read throughput” and “pure Go (no cgo)” as deliberate design goals. If you want the graph-database connection, it is the same story as Neo4j: a purpose-built engine, except here the graph system (Dgraph) is layered on top of a general KV core. And if you want the Go-native LSM contrast from the transactional world, CockroachDB’s Pebble re-implements the classic design, while Badger re-thinks it.

In this tour we read the main branch of dgraph-io/badger (the v4 module line) from DB.Open to compaction, with two generated architecture diagrams. Everything cited below was verified against the actual source tree.

Overview: the write path flows from a client transaction through the oracle and a single write channel into the value log and memtable; flushing and compaction build SSTs that the read path merges back together.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup and state. Open, L195 replays the manifest, opens memtables and the value log, and starts flush and compaction goroutines. The DB struct, L82 holds the active memtable mt, immutable imm, the vlog, and the writeCh channel.
  • Transactions. NewTransaction, L757 pulls a read timestamp from the oracle, L24, the SSI authority that also tracks committed keys for conflict detection.
  • Commit. commitAndSend, L521 passes hasConflict, L128, gets a commit version from newCommitTs, L153, and hands entries to the write channel.
  • Value log first. writeRequests, L868 sends writes through vlog.write, L817; the LSM receives only a 16-byte-ish valuePointer, L15 of {fid, offset, len}.
  • Memtable. memTable.Put, L170 encodes a WAL record via logFile.encodeEntry, L283, then inserts into Skiplist.Put, L273, which bump-allocates nodes in an Arena, L26.
  • Flush. flushMemtable, L1151 drains full memtables into SSTs via Builder.Add, L332, then addLevel0Table, L1656 registers them in L0.
  • Compaction and metadata. doCompact, L1604 runs picked priorities through subcompact, L691 and compactBuildTables, L935, journaling results as a Manifest, L36 change set.
  • Reads. Txn.Get, L434 resolves to db.get, L789, which probes memtables then levelsController.get, L1721; scans use NewMergeIterator, L198 and missing values are fetched by valueLog.Read, L965.

Detail: each node is a grep-verified function or type in the badger source tree; follow the edges to see how a write becomes a memtable entry, an SST block, and finally a readable item.

WiscKey: Why the Value Log Exists

Badger’s defining idea is the WiscKey split. Classic LSM engines like RocksDB and LevelDB inline values into SSTs, so every compaction rewrites them — expensive when values are large. Badger appends values to append-only log files instead. The valueLog struct, L462 keeps a map of files and a head file for writes; vlog.write, L817 validates the batch, appends to the head file, and returns value pointers that the LSM stores in place of bytes. Only entries whose value exceeds ValueThreshold are spilled this way, and the default threshold is 1 MB (maxValueThreshold, options.go, L201), so in practice almost every meaningful value lives in the log. Files roll at roughly 1 GB (ValueLogFileSize, options.go, L165).

The cost of the split is garbage. Rewriting a log file to reclaim space is vlog.rewrite, L162, which streams live entries back into fresh files; users trigger it explicitly with RunValueLogGC, L1304 passing a discard ratio. There is also an adaptive vlogThreshold, L1138 that can tune the spill threshold from observed write sizes.

Durability defaults are tuned for throughput over latency: SyncWrites is false by default (options.go, L143), so callers needing a hard durability point call DB.Sync, L708, which syncs the memtable’s WAL and the value log. Every value-log record carries a CRC anyway, and the replay side (safeRead, L61) re-verifies it when entries are decoded back into memory.

The Write Path: SSI Transactions to Skiplist

Badger guarantees concurrent ACID transactions with serializable snapshot isolation, and the mechanism is compact enough to read in one sitting. oracle.readTs, L78 snapshots the world for a new transaction; oracle.hasConflict, L128 compares that snapshot against keys committed since; oracle.newCommitTs, L153 assigns the final version. Conflict detection is on by default (DetectConflicts: true, options.go, L175) and can be disabled per-database for read-mostly workloads.

Every key is physically versioned: KeyWithTs, L113 appends an 8-byte timestamp to the user key, ParseTs, L121 peels it back, and CompareKeys, L132 orders by key first, version descending. That is why a “3D access (key-value-version)” row appears in the README comparison table — iterators can walk all versions of a key.

Backpressure is explicit. ensureRoomForWrite, L1044 blocks writes when too many memtables or L0 tables pile up: defaults are NumMemtables: 5, NumLevelZeroTables: 5, and stall at NumLevelZeroTablesStall: 15 (options.go, L128-140). Progress accounting runs through the generic WaterMark, L51, whose WaitForMark, L104 lets goroutines wait until all earlier work has finished — the same primitive backs transaction and compaction sequencing. The Throttle, L187 in y gates in-flight batches. One detail worth noting: the commit path batches aggressively. doWrites, L943 coalesces whatever requests have piled up in the channel and writes them out together, so hundreds of small transactions can share a single value-log append and a single memtable fill — one of the reasons Badger sustains very high write throughput in the benchmarks the README links.

SST Format: Blocks, Flatbuffer Index, Bloom Filters

The SST builder (Builder, L68) accumulates 4 KB blocks (BlockSize, default in DefaultOptions, L123), prefix-compresses keys against their predecessor, and closes a block in finishBlock, L262 when shouldFinishBlock says so. Per-block CRCs guard against silent corruption. buildIndex, L526 then serializes block offsets, key counts, and max versions as a flatbuffer (the generated Go lives in fb/), followed by a bloom filter built with NewFilter, L45 at a false-positive rate of 0.01. On read, DoesNotHave, L699 rejects tables cheaply before any block is touched.

Reading an SST is mmap-first: OpenTable, L268 memory-maps the file and parses the index, while Table.block, L552 fetches cached blocks (a 256 MB block cache is the default) and binary-searches them with the blockIterator, L18. Range scans stack per-level iterators into the heap-based merge iterator, and the DB-level machinery that stitches memtables plus levels together lives in appendIterators, L1768. Because tables inside levels below L0 do not overlap, scans fold each level’s tables into one ConcatIterator, L426 that steps through them in key order (the L1+ branch of appendIterators, L365). Point lookups take a cheaper route: bloom check first, then a per-table iterator Seek (level_handler.go, L308). If you are paranoid about bit rot, VerifyChecksum, L698 re-hashes every block of every table on demand.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps setup minimal, and it matches what we verified in the tree. Badger v3+ requires Go 1.23 or above and go modules; from your project run go get github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4, which fetches the library as an embedded dependency. For offline maintenance tooling (backup, restore, flatten, info), the README shows installing the CLI from the repository’s badger subdirectory with cd badger followed by go install ., which drops a badger binary into your $GOBIN.

A minimal feature-record write, using only API surface we verified above, looks like this:

import badger "github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4"

db, err := badger.Open(badger.DefaultOptions("/tmp/feature-store"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer db.Close()

txn := db.NewTransaction(true) // read-write; gets readTs from the oracle
if err := txn.Set([]byte("emb:user:42"), vectorBytes); err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := txn.Commit(); err != nil {
    return err
}

DefaultOptions is a good starting point: 64 MB memtables, snappy compression, and a 256 MB block cache. For bulk loads, prefer the write batch API (NewWriteBatch, L39, flushed with WriteBatch.Flush, L211); for online model training loops that read at fixed versions, managed mode’s NewTransactionAt, L23 pins a snapshot. Large parallel dumps and restores can use the streaming interfaces (Stream.Orchestrate, L415 and StreamWriter.Flush, L252), which fan work across goroutines.

Honest Limits

Badger is a KV library, not a database server. There is no SQL layer, no secondary indexes, and no query language — you get Get, Set, Delete, iteration, and versions; anything richer you build yourself (or take from Dgraph, BadgerHold, and friends). It is embedded and single-node: there is no built-in network protocol or replication, so high availability is your job, typically via raft-backed wrappers. There is a pure in-memory mode (an InMemory option gates all value-log and file I/O, as seen at value.go, L818), handy for ephemeral caches and tests, but it is still a library, not a service.

Operationally, the WiscKey trade cuts both ways. Value-log garbage needs periodic, explicit GC (RunValueLogGC, L1304), and picking the discard ratio is a judgment call. The tuning surface is large — Options, L31 exposes dozens of knobs from MemTableSize to NumCompactors: 4 and MaxLevels: 7 — and wrong settings show up as stalls rather than errors. Versioned keys mean a naive iterator can see multiple versions per key unless NumVersionsToKeep and iterator options are set deliberately. Finally, the README’s platform table notes real caveats: directory fsync is unsupported on AIX, file locking differs on Windows, and Plan9/WASM lack locking — worth reading dir_*.go before unusual deployments. Documentation is serviceable but thin (the in-repo docs/ folder plus badger.dgraph.io), so the source, as always, is the real manual — much easier to read here than in C++, and a good companion to Pebble if you are comparing Go LSM designs.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of BadgerDB, the pure-Go WiscKey-based LSM key-value store behind Dgraph, covering transactions, skiplist memtables, the value log, compaction, and the manifest.

entry.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

link.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

entry.content:
If you are serving AI features to users in several regions at once, you eventually hit the same wall: a single-node Postgres works beautifully until you need writes to survive a datacenter failure, or until feature data, embeddings metadata, and audit trails have to stay transactionally consistent across continents. CockroachDB is the open-source answer that industry keeps reaching for — a distributed SQL database written in Go that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, scales horizontally by splitting data into replicated ranges, and refuses to lose an acknowledged write even when machines are failing underneath it. For ML platforms specifically, it is a natural backing store for regional feature stores, vector-metadata joins, and anything where a stale or lost row quietly corrupts a model’s inputs.

What makes it fascinating to read at the source level is how little magic there is. Everything reduces to one repeated loop: a SQL statement becomes a transactional batch of key-value requests, that batch is routed to a leaseholder replica, the replica evaluates it against multi-version MVCC state, the result is replicated through Raft, and the whole thing rests on an LSM-tree engine called Pebble. If you have followed our earlier storage-engine tours of RocksDB and LevelDB, you will feel at home immediately — Pebble is the direct Go descendant of that same LSM lineage, purpose-built by Cockroach Labs when they outgrew embedding RocksDB as a C++ library inside their Go process.

In this tour we read the actual code in the cockroachdb/cockroach monorepo and draw two architecture diagrams from it: an overview of the full query path, and a detailed map of the functions that make it work. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the current master branch, so the links drop you straight into the source.

Overview: one query's journey from a Postgres-compatible socket to replicated LSM storage. Every edge is a real call path in the Go source.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A session is just a wire protocol. The pgwire conn struct (conn, L59) accepts the same PostgreSQL frontend/backend protocol that Postgres speaks, so existing drivers connect with zero code changes. Server.ServeConn (ServeConn, L991) upgrades each connection into a SQL session.
  • Sessions run a state machine. connExecutor (connExecutor, L1609) owns transaction state, and execStmt (execStmt, L123) with execStmtInOpenState (execStmtInOpenState, L417) drive every statement through it.
  • Every query is optimized, not interpreted. planner.makeOptimizerPlan (makeOptimizerPlan, L298) builds a memo of alternative plans and prices them; coster.ComputeCost (coster.ComputeCost, L526) is where join orders and index choices actually get decided.
  • Plans become physical flows. The PhysicalPlan (PhysicalPlan, L125) assigns operators to nodes, and flows of ProcessorBase instances (ProcessorBase, L345) execute them locally or distributed.
  • SQL touches data only through KV. Row sources end up in Txn.Send (Txn.Send, L1386), which funnels batches into the TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) for intent tracking and retries.
  • Batches are routed, not broadcast. DistSender.Send (DistSender.Send, L1310) splits a BatchRequest by key range and sendToReplicas (sendToReplicas, L2669) targets each range’s leaseholder replica over gRPC.
  • One Node fronts one process. Inbound RPCs land in Node.batchInternal (batchInternal, L1648), which hands work to the Store (Store, L909) that owns replicas on local disks.
  • Replicas evaluate, then replicate. The Replica (Replica, L365) evaluates the batch under its lease, and evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) proposes the result to Raft so a majority durably agrees.
  • Everything ends in Pebble. The Pebble engine (Pebble, L884) implements the Engine interface (Engine, L932) and persists both the Raft log and the MVCC keyspace.

The detailed map: 34 components from wire protocol to LSM compactions, with the exact functions that glue each layer to the next.

SQL: From Wire Protocol to Costed Memo

The SQL layer’s discipline is striking: there is exactly one optimizer, and nothing bypasses it. optbuilder.Builder.Build (Builder.Build, L263) converts the parsed AST into a memo — a DAG of relational expressions where equivalent alternatives share groups. The xform explorer then applies transformation rules via exploreGroup (exploreGroup, L155) until the Coster (coster.ComputeCost, L526) can no longer find a cheaper expression. Cost here is not an abstract score: it is calibrated in units of IO, CPU, and memory (the Cost type lives in Cost, L17), which is why the optimizer can reason sensibly about wide scans of embedding tables versus narrow index lookups on feature keys.

Execution follows the same decomposition. dispatchToExecutionEngine (dispatchToExecutionEngine, L2887) picks between local and distributed plans, execWithDistSQLEngine (execWithDistSQLEngine, L3664) sets up flows, and each node runs its fragment through the Flow interface (Flow, L72). Processors stream rows to each other rather than materializing whole tables — the same pull-based style that makes DuckDB-class engines cache-friendly.

KV: TxnCoordSender and the DistSender

Beneath SQL, CockroachDB is a transactional key-value store, and the client side of that store is small enough to hold in your head. kv.DB (DB, L272) hands out Txn handles; batches stage operations like Batch.Put (Batch.Put, L460) as kvpb requests. The TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) is the transaction’s brain: it records which ranges hold intents, heartbeats the transaction record so other nodes can tell a live writer from a crashed one, and orchestrates retries.

The DistSender (DistSender, L726) then does geography: it consults the range metadata to find which leaseholder serves each key span, splits the batch accordingly, and re-runs pieces when ranges split or leaders move mid-flight. By default every transaction runs at SERIALIZABLE isolation — the strongest level Postgres only offers opt-in — implemented through MVCC timestamps and read refreshes rather than lock tables.

Replication: Ranges, Leases, and Raft

Each range (a contiguous key span, default 512 MiB) is owned by a Replica on each of its three or more voting stores. Exactly one replica holds the lease at a time; pendingLeaseRequest.requestLease (requestLease, L552) and its async variant (requestLeaseAsync, L474) make acquisition cooperative and liveness-aware. Only the leaseholder may serve consistent reads, which is why the diagram routes every batch through it.

Writes then follow classic Raft. evaluateBatch (evaluateBatch, L198) runs the batch against current state to produce a result; evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) turns that into a proposed command with a MaxLeaseIndex for replay protection; propose (propose, L411) enqueues it; and handleRaftReady (handleRaftReady, L867) drains the ready data into the log and transport. The consensus algorithm itself lives in the vendored pkg/raft library (raft, L305), a heavily-evolved descendant of etcd’s raft. Acknowledgment waits for a majority, so a range survives losing a minority of its replicas with no human intervention.

Storage: MVCC over a Pebble LSM

The storage engine contract is the Engine interface (Engine, L932) — a versioned reader/writer — and Pebble is its production implementation (Pebble, L884). MVCC keys are literally user keys suffixed with wall-clock timestamps, so MVCCGet (MVCCGet, L1401) and MVCCPut (MVCCPut, L1923) are LSM operations over that encoding, with mvccPutInternal (mvccPutInternal, L2251) deciding between values and tombstoned intents. Scans merge intents and versions through pebbleMVCCScanner (pebbleMVCCScanner, L381).

This is the part of the codebase our series has been circling for months: Pebble takes the LSM ideas RocksDB refined from LevelDB — memtables, tiered SSTables, bloom filters, compactions — and re-implements them in pure Go, adding level-aware write amplification control that suits CockroachDB’s raft-append-heavy workload. Reading pkg/storage right after those two codebases is a genuinely satisfying experience.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything below comes straight from the repository’s own README. The quickest route is a pre-built binary: the README’s “Starting with CockroachDB” list points at the documented installer page for your platform. If you would rather build from source, the README’s “Building from source” section defers to the project wiki; expect a Bazel-driven build — the repo’s GNUmakefile is a thin wrapper whose build target just runs ./dev build, and ./dev in turn drives Bazel. Budget real time and disk for the first compile; this is a large monorepo with C dependencies.

Once you have a cockroach binary: start a local demo cluster with three nodes as the README suggests, open the built-in SQL client, create a database and table, and then connect your application with any PostgreSQL driver or ORM — the README explicitly notes that the PostgreSQL wire protocol is supported, so psycopg2, asyncpg, or SQLAlchemy all work unchanged. For an ML service, your first schema might be a features table keyed by entity ID with an _updated_at column, giving you transactional feature reads alongside the labels you train on.

Honest Limits

Read the license before you plan around it. Since the v24.3 series (releases after November 18, 2024, per the README’s licensing section), the code ships under the CockroachDB Software License rather than an OSI-approved open-source license: the LICENSE file grants use and modification for operating, testing, and improving CockroachDB, but prohibits offering it as a commercial DBaaS without a license key. Source-available, yes; fully open-source, no. For an internal AI platform this is usually irrelevant, but check it before embedding.

Engineering costs are real, too. The monorepo is enormous (over 20,000 tracked files), builds run through Bazel with a custom ./dev tool, and running a production cluster means operating at least three nodes, monitoring Raft health, and accepting that every write pays a consensus round-trip. It is a server, not an embeddable library — there is no “just link it into your app” mode like SQLite’s. For single-region workloads that fit in one machine, plain Postgres remains simpler; for battery-backup-grade regional consistency, that trade is exactly what you are buying.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of CockroachDB's Go monorepo, tracing a query from the PostgreSQL wire protocol through the cost-based optimizer, the DistSender, Raft replication, and down into the Pebble LSM storage engine.

entry.title: Dolt Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Git for Data

link.title: Dolt Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Git for Data

entry.content:
Every serious ML effort eventually collides with the same question: which exact rows did this model train on? Training data is not static. Labels get corrected, schemas grow columns, bad batches are rolled back, and feature-engineering experiments fork the dataset in different directions. File-based snapshots — folders of CSV or Parquet dumps — cannot answer lineage questions cleanly, and homegrown version columns rot fast. Dolt takes the radically honest approach: it is a real SQL database where every data revision is a commit, and the whole toolbox you know from Git — clone, branch, merge, diff, push, pull — applies to tables. Where table-format projects such as Apache Iceberg version files and snapshots in object storage, Dolt versions the rows themselves, inside a transactional SQL engine, down to per-cell history queries.

The practical hook is compatibility. Dolt speaks the MySQL wire protocol, so existing clients, connectors and BI tools attach to it like any MySQL server, while version control shows up as SQL system tables (dolt_log, dolt_status, dolt_diff_<table>) and stored procedures (dolt_add, dolt_commit, dolt_merge). The project’s own README compresses the idea into one line: “Git versions files. Dolt versions tables.” For ML teams this means dataset audits, branch-and-merge feature experiments, and push/pull collaboration with the operational model of Git but the query power of SQL — no new export formats, no sidecar metadata store.

In this tour we read the actual source of dolthub/dolt on the main branch (verified at commit f16514116453), walking from the MySQL entry points down to the chunk store, then zooming into the mechanics that make versioned tables fast: Prolly Trees, content addressing, and the commit machinery. Every symbol below was checked against the tree at that commit.

Overview: queries enter through the CLI or the MySQL-compatible server, flow through the SQL engine and version core, and land as rows in Prolly Trees whose chunks are persisted by the Noms block store alongside commit objects.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SqlCmd, L114 implements dolt sql, the interactive shell and one-off query mode that ships inside the single binary.
  • SqlServerCmd, L162 starts the MySQL-wire-compatible server, so any MySQL client can connect without knowing versioning exists.
  • DoltSession, L50 carries per-connection state — current database, branch, transaction — bridging SQL sessions onto version control.
  • RootValue, L59 is the immutable snapshot interface: table names resolved to table values, the object every query reads and every commit pins.
  • DoltDB, L128 is the version-control facade; its Resolve, L532 turns a CommitSpec like HEAD~ into a concrete commit.
  • Map (prolly.Map), L32 is the Prolly Tree map holding encoded row tuples, with Get, L264 for point lookups.
  • Node, L40 and the NodeStore, L38 interface manage the immutable tree nodes that give Prolly Trees their structural sharing.
  • ChunkStore, L74 is the content-addressed persistence contract, implemented on disk by NomsBlockStore, L97.
  • Dataset, L468 models refs — branches and working sets — whose heads point at commit objects, the final layer of the stack.

Detail: CLI verbs map onto staging and commit actions; the engine reads roots and prolly-backed indexes; mutations flush through the tree mutator into chunks, the manifest, the journal and table files.

Prolly Trees: Chunks With Structural Sharing

The storage story starts at the bottom. A Chunk, L33 is simply a byte slice plus its content hash — Dolt inherits this unit from the Noms project it credits in its README. Hashes are fixed-size Hash, L80 values, so every object in the system is addressed by the cryptographic digest of its content. Writes never mutate existing chunks; new content means new chunks with new addresses.

Prolly Trees are the clever part. A Node, L40 is an immutable tree node whose leaves hold key/value tuples, and node boundaries are chosen probabilistically from content — which is what makes the tree “prolly” (probabilistic B-tree). When you edit a map you do not touch it directly: Mutate, L216 hands you a MutableMap, L54 (an alias for the generic GenericMutableMap) that accumulates edits, with Put, L123 and delete operations buffered before flush. Flushing runs ApplyMutations, L63, which rewrites only the paths of the tree that changed, serializing each new node through NewProllyMapSerializer, L43. Because interior nodes address their children by hash, unchanged subtrees are physically shared between any two versions of the map.

That single design decision is why Dolt can diff, merge and time-travel cheaply. Two commits differ exactly in the chunks that differ, and merges reuse the common ancestor’s shared nodes. It is a different trade-off from the LSM engines of RocksDB, which optimize for write amplification on mutable data; Dolt optimizes for cheap immutable versions of mutable data.

Commits, Refs and the Version Core

Above storage sits the Git-like object model. The string you type — HEAD~, a branch name, a commit hash — is parsed by NewCommitSpec, L97 into a CommitSpec, L64; the ~ and ^ suffixes are split off by SplitAncestorSpec, L109 into an AncestorSpec, L80. Resolve, L532 then walks refs to produce a Commit, L49 — the familiar trio of parent hashes, a root pointer, and metadata.

The working-copy model maps cleanly onto tables. WorkingSet, L316 holds the working, staged and head roots for a branch. dolt add triggers StageTables, L26, copying table roots from the working root to the staged root; dolt commit goes through GetCommitStaged, L80, which validates constraints and builds the commit with NewCommitMeta, L129 capturing author, email and message. Refs themselves are Dataset, L468 values managed by the Database, L51 layer, and CommitValue, L568 atomically swaps a head to the new commit. History queries such as dolt_log read back metadata with GetCommitMeta, L428.

The SQL Surface: Sessions, Indexes and the Wire

The engine integration is where Dolt stops feeling like Git bolted onto a database. DoltSession, L50 binds each connection to a database session state, and the adapter in go/libraries/doltcore/sqle/database.go exposes dolt databases to the GMS SQL analyzer so standard queries, joins and transactions behave as you expect. Secondary indexes are Prolly Trees too — index scans run through prollyIndexIter, L34, and table structure is described by the Schema, L43 interface of columns, primary keys and index collections.

The wire path matters for ML workflows because it is how Python reaches the data: SqlServerCmd, L162 starts the server, and from there a plain mysql client or any MySQL driver can query dolt_history_<table> for row-level lineage. We compared the MySQL server codebase itself in our MySQL source tour; Dolt’s approach is the opposite end — reimplementing the protocol surface natively in Go rather than carrying the C++ server.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps onboarding deliberately boring, which is a feature. Install the single binary — roughly 103 MB — via the release install script for Linux/macOS, brew install dolt on Mac, the .msi or choco install dolt on Windows, or build from source inside the repo’s go directory with go install ./cmd/dolt (Go plus a C toolchain, since Dolt depends on cgo). Configure your identity exactly like Git: dolt config --global --add user.email you@domain.com and the matching user.name.

Then create your first versioned dataset:

mkdir ml-datasets && cd ml-datasets
dolt init
dolt sql -q "create table training_runs (id int primary key, model varchar(255), row_count int)"
dolt add training_runs
dolt commit -m "initial training_runs schema"

dolt init creates the empty data repository, dolt sql -q runs one query and exits, and add/commit stage and record table changes. From Python you can connect with any MySQL library, run inserts between training epochs, and commit checkpoints — every snapshot of the dataset is now addressable. The README also shows the SQL-procedure equivalents for server-side use: call dolt_add('training_runs') and call dolt_commit('-m', 'message'), with dolt_log, dolt_status and dolt_diff_<table> as inspection points. Branches work identically: call dolt_checkout('-b', 'feature-experiment'), mutate and commit, then call dolt_merge('feature-experiment') back into main — the README’s walkthrough demonstrates the full round trip, including as of time-travel queries against a branch.

Honest Limits

Dolt’s compatibility claim deserves precision. The README recommends MySQL clients up to version 8.4 and notes that MySQL 9.0’s caching_sha2_password authentication needs extra configuration to connect; the server also identifies itself as 5.7.9-Vitess, a nod to the Vitess-derived SQL engine, so scripts that sniff server versions can be surprised. Compatibility is broad — foreign keys, secondary indexes, triggers, checks and stored procedures are supported per the README — but it is not bit-for-bit MySQL parity.

The versioning superpowers are not free. Content addressing and structural sharing add bookkeeping that a plain B-tree engine serving purely mutable OLTP data does not pay, and the write path funnels through chunk flushes rather than in-place page updates. The distribution model has its own footprint: one Go binary of about 103 MB, a large Go monorepo (several thousand files at HEAD), and a cgo dependency for building from source. If your dialect is Postgres rather than MySQL, the README points to the separate Doltgres project, which is in Beta. None of these are disqualifiers for the dataset-versioning niche; they are the price of putting Git semantics inside a transactional SQL engine.

What to Steal for Your Own Stack

Three ideas transfer well beyond Dolt. First, content addressing as the substrate: if every object’s name is its hash, diffing, deduplication and integrity checks fall out of the design for free — the same insight behind LevelDB-style immutable table files, here taken to the whole database. Second, structural sharing: probabilistic node splitting is what turns “store every snapshot” from wasteful to nearly free, a technique any snapshot-heavy system can borrow. Third, the session-root design: keeping working, staged and head roots per branch (WorkingSet, L316) is a clean pattern for any system that needs drafts, staging and published state as first-class data. Dolt is the rare database whose source reads like an argument that version control is a storage-engine property, not a bolt-on feature — and for ML data workflows, that argument lands.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of dolthub/dolt, the MySQL-compatible SQL database that versions tables with content-addressed Prolly Trees, commits, branches and merges.

entry.title: LevelDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Engine That Started It All

link.title: LevelDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Engine That Started It All

entry.content:
Yesterday we walked the RocksDB source tree — the heavily forked engine that powers Flink state stores, Kafka Streams, TiKV, and the local segments of countless vector databases. But RocksDB did not appear out of nothing. It is a fork of LevelDB, the compact key-value library written at Google by Sanjay Ghemawat and Jeff Dean. The README describes it modestly: “a fast key-value storage library written at Google that provides an ordered mapping from string keys to string values.” Behind that one line sits the first widely read implementation of the log-structured merge (LSM) architecture — append-only writes, sorted in-memory tables, immutable disk files, and background compaction. Every storage engine that calls itself LSM today is quoting this codebase, usually without attribution.

Why should an ML or data-infrastructure engineer care about a ~20k-line C++ library? Because embedded KV stores are the substrate under a surprising amount of AI plumbing. Feature stores and data-preparation jobs use them as durable, ordered dictionaries for raw events and materialized features. On-device inference stacks use them as local caches and model registries, and the browser world famously runs on this lineage too — Chrome’s IndexedDB is backed by LevelDB, which means every offline-first ML web app ultimately reads and writes one of these files. Stream-processing frameworks checkpoint operator state into RocksDB descendants of this exact design. Once you understand how LevelDB turns a Put into a log record, a skiplist insert, and eventually a sorted string table, half the storage engines you will ever debug become familiar.

This post tours google/leveldb at its main branch, verified line by line in the actual source. Two diagrams anchor the tour: an overview of the full write-and-read cycle, and a detail view that expands into the individual functions. All paths below are repo-relative, so you can open any link and land on the exact function we discuss.

The complete LevelDB cycle: every write is logged, absorbed by a skiplist memtable, spilled into an immutable Level-0 SSTable, merged across levels by background compaction, and coordinated through the version set and MANIFEST file. Reads probe the newest structures first.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • DBImpl::Write, L1206 is the only write entry point. It queues the writer, merges concurrent small batches via DBImpl::BuildBatchGroup, L1281, and performs the canonical LSM handshake: log first, memory second.
  • log::Writer::AddRecord, L34 appends the batch to the write-ahead log, fragmenting records across 32KB physical blocks with per-fragment CRC checksums.
  • WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto, L132 replays the batch through a handler that lands each operation in the memtable via MemTable::Add, L76 — keys stamped with a sequence number and a value-or-deletion type tag.
  • DBImpl::MakeRoomForWrite, L1331 enforces the 4MB memtable budget (write_buffer_size, options.h, L83) and switches the active memtable to immutable before handing writes to a fresh one.
  • DBImpl::WriteLevel0Table, L505 and BuildTable, L17 flush the immutable memtable into a brand-new SSTable using TableBuilder::Add, L94, which emits restart-point compressed data blocks.
  • DBImpl::BackgroundCompaction, L708 runs on a single background thread, consuming the compaction score computed by VersionSet::PickCompaction, L1252.
  • VersionSet::LogAndApply, L777 publishes every file-level change — flushes and compactions alike — as a VersionEdit appended to the MANIFEST.
  • DBImpl::Get, L1121 probes memtable, immutable memtable, then the live file set through Version::Get, L324, newest structure first, stopping at the first match.

The detail view expands each stage into its constituent functions: batch grouping and replay, the skiplist-plus-arena memory stack, 32KB log blocks and recovery, the SSTable format from TableBuilder to BlockIter, the level-by-level read probe, score-driven compaction, and the bloom-filter and LRU-cache shields that keep reads off disk.

The Write Path: Log First, Skiplist Second

The elegance of DBImpl::Write is its group-commit queue. Each calling thread registers a Writer on a deque and sleeps until it reaches the front. The leader then calls BuildBatchGroup to absorb pending writers into one merged batch (capped at 1MB, plus 128KB when the first batch is small), stamps it with the next sequence numbers, and — with the lock released — appends it via log_->AddRecord and applies it through WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto. This is why a single-item write and a thousand-item batch cost roughly the same number of fsyncs: batching is the engine’s answer to write amplification at the front door.

The memtable itself is a skiplist, not a balanced tree. SkipList::Insert, L55 relies on the arena allocator (Arena::AllocateAligned, L38) so that nodes are only reclaimed wholesale when the entire memtable dies. MemTable::Add encodes each entry as key length | sequence<<8 | type | key | value length | value, which makes iteration order deterministic even for duplicate user keys. Readers traverse the same structure with MemTable::Get, L102, and the exported MemTableIterator, L46 doubles as a compaction input.

Recovery is the mirror image: at open time, DBImpl::RecoverLogFile, L385 replays the last WAL into a fresh memtable, which is why every committed Put survives a crash even though the memtable was pure memory.

Reading: One Probe, Three Frontiers, Then Levels

DBImpl::Get assembles a LookupKey with the current sequence number and hands it to Version::Get, L324. Level 0 is special: its files can overlap each other, so all of them are searched newest-first. From level 1 upward, files are key-disjoint, and the version binary-searches for the single file whose range brackets the key — typically one file touched per level. Before any data block is read, the bloom filter answers cheaply: FilterBlockReader::KeyMayMatch, L90 consults a per-block filter built from BloomFilterPolicy, L17 at roughly ten bits per key, so absent keys skip both the file read and the block decode.

When a block is actually needed, TableCache::Get, L100 opens the file through Table::Open, L38, and Table::InternalGet, L214 seeks the index block, loads the data block, and scans it with the iterator from Block::NewIterator, L280. Two caches amortize this work: the table cache holds open file handles, and ShardedLRUCache, L353 — sixteen independent LRU lists with LRUCache::Insert, L268 as the hot path — keeps decompressed blocks in memory. The README’s own db_bench numbers make the effect concrete: readrandom improves from about 60,000 to about 190,000 reads per second once compaction and block caching warm up.

Iteration composes the same pieces: NewMergingIterator, L179 unions the memtable iterator with one iterator per file level, and DBIter, L39 filters internal keys and tombstones so the user sees a clean ordered view. Telemetry hooks like DBImpl::GetApproximateSizes, L1469 round out the API by summing file sizes overlapping a key range — the same primitive monitoring tools use to chart database growth.

Compaction and the Version Set

Compaction is where LSM engines earn their name. VersionSet::PickCompaction, L1252 scores every level and picks the worst offender; Level 0 compacts when it accumulates four files, while deeper levels compact on a size ratio. DBImpl::DoCompactionWork, L898 then merges the inputs with a MergingIterator, dropping entries shadowed by newer versions or tombstones (it consults Compaction::IsBaseLevelForKey to know whether a tombstone can finally be discarded) and writing outputs sized to the level’s file budget — 2MB default files per max_file_size in options.h, L116.

Every mutation of the file universe flows through VersionSet::LogAndApply, L777. The new file lists are assembled by VersionSet::Builder::SaveTo, L672 into a successor Version, the edit is appended to the MANIFEST, and the immutable old version stays alive for any reader still holding a snapshot. This copy-on-write versioning is what makes lock-free reads and consistent snapshots coexist with a mutating database — a design RocksDB inherited wholesale.

From Install to Your First Model

LevelDB builds with CMake out of the box. The README’s POSIX quick start is two commands:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/google/leveldb.git
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release .. && cmake --build .

On Windows, generate a Visual Studio solution with cmake -G "Visual Studio 15 Win64" .. and build it with devenv /build Debug leveldb.sln. Link against the resulting library (and Snappy for compression) and you have your first feature store in a few lines — the same API surface verified in db.h, L53 and options.h, L50:

leveldb::DB* db;
leveldb::Options options;
options.create_if_missing = true;
leveldb::Status s = leveldb::DB::Open(options, "features.db", &db);
db->Put(leveldb::WriteOptions(), "feature:user:42", payload);
std::string value;
db->Get(leveldb::ReadOptions(), "feature:user:42", &value);

Wrap this in Python via one of the mature bindings and you can log training features, deduplicate corpus shards by content hash, or persist inference results with byte-range ordering for free.

Honest Limits

The README is refreshingly blunt about scope, and these limits are exactly why forks exist. LevelDB is not a SQL database — no relational model, no query language, no secondary indexes; you bring the schema logic. Only a single process (possibly multi-threaded) may open a database at a time, and there is no client-server support: networked deployments must wrap their own server. The maintenance posture is worth respecting too — the repository now accepts only critical-bug fixes, so it is a design reference more than a moving product. Operationally, the cost model is asymmetric: the README’s benchmark shows fillsync at 0.4 MB/s versus 62.7 MB/s without per-write syncs, and background compaction trades write latency spikes for read speed — the very tradeoff that RocksDB later tuned with threads and rate limiting, and that LSM-descended time-series engines like the one behind InfluxDB’s storage redesign reshaped for their own workloads.

If you want to go deeper, compare this tour with our RocksDB source walkthrough to see what the fork changed — column families, pluggable memtables, compaction strategies — and with SQLite, the other single-process embedded classic, which chose a B-tree instead of an LSM. Vector-database readers will recognize the pattern too: projects like Milvus build their local mutable-state persistence on RocksDB’s LSM files, the direct descendants of everything diagrammed above.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of google/leveldb tracing the write path, skiplist memtable, WAL, SSTable format, compaction scoring and version sets of the original LSM storage engine.

entry.title: Inside MySQL: A Source-Level Tour of InnoDB, the Optimizer, and Replication

link.title: Inside MySQL: A Source-Level Tour of InnoDB, the Optimizer, and Replication

entry.content:
MySQL is the quiet backbone of the internet. Written in C and C++, maintained by Oracle in the open on GitHub, it has spent three decades being the default transactional database behind forums, e-commerce carts, payment ledgers, and SaaS dashboards. Its storage engine, InnoDB, delivers full ACID transactions, crash recovery through a write-ahead log, and row-level locking — all in a codebase you can clone, grep, and read end to end. For this tour I rendered two architecture diagrams of mysql/mysql-server directly from the source tree, and every claim below links to a real file and line in the repository.

Why should AI engineers care about a 1990s-era SQL server? Because almost every serious LLM application needs one. When your chatbot writes conversation history, your recommendation service logs features, or your billing layer records inference credits, you want a store that is consistent under concurrent writes and survivable across restarts — that is MySQL’s home turf. Feature stores, annotation queues, agent memory, and evaluation harnesses all start as rows in an OLTP table long before anything reaches a vector index. Teams often pair MySQL with Redis as a cache and key-value layer in front of it, or replicate change events into Kafka to feed downstream model training and streaming feature computation. And if you come from the PostgreSQL world, reading MySQL’s source is the fastest way to understand why the two ecosystem cultures differ so much.

The version I read is the development branch: git ls-remote shows the default branch is trunk, and the MYSQL_VERSION file reports 26.10.0-INNOVATION with previous LTS 9.7.0 — so this is moving, forward-looking code, not a packaged release. The full tree lists roughly 61,000 files; I checked out only sql (the server core), storage/innobase (InnoDB), mysys, and libbinlogevents for the diagrams. Here is the big picture, from the network socket down to disk.

MySQL request flow: from mysqld's connection loop through the SQL layer and InnoDB to the binary log and replica threads. Rendered from the trunk tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot and accept. mysqld_main, L9206 initializes engines and enters the connection event loop; each accepted socket goes through Connection_handler_manager::process_new_connection, L262, which hands it to a per-connection handler.
  • Speak the wire protocol. Protocol_classic::get_command, L2890 reads one packet and decodes the COM_* command byte that drives everything else.
  • Parse the query. dispatch_command, L1748 switches on that byte; for COM_QUERY it tokenizes via lex_one_token, L1490 and feeds the bison grammar.
  • Plan it. JOIN::optimize, L344 picks join order, access methods, and temp-table strategies per query block.
  • Compile to iterators. CreateIteratorFromAccessPath, L696 turns the declarative plan into a tree of RowIterator objects, executed by Query_expression::ExecuteIteratorQuery, L1068.
  • Cross the engine boundary. The executor pulls rows through handler::ha_index_read_map, L3390 — the portable storage-engine interface — and writes rows through ha_write_row.
  • Inside InnoDB. Reads funnel into row_search_mvcc, L4437, pages are fetched by buf_page_get_gen, L4473 in the buffer pool, and durability comes from the redo log writer thread.
  • Replicate it. Commit goes through MYSQL_BIN_LOG::ordered_commit, L7530 for binlog group commit, and a dump thread streams events to replica I/O threads.

The detail diagram zooms into the parts that make MySQL genuinely interesting under load: the iterator executor, the InnoDB B-tree and buffer pool machinery, mini-transactions, MVCC, and the three-stage commit.

Internal detail: how a query becomes iterators, how InnoDB pages and redo interact, and how group commit coordinates binlog and engine commits.

From Install to Your First Model

Suppose you want this stack running so an AI service can start writing rows to it. The README in the repo is famously minimal — thirteen lines that state this is a release of MySQL, an SQL database server, and point you at the canonical places: downloads at dev.mysql.com/downloads and documentation at dev.mysql.com/doc. Binary packages from that page are the realistic path for production. If you want to read along with source instead, clone the GitHub repo and build with CMake — the root CMakeLists.txt is the entry point, and the Docs directory in the tree carries the generated documentation sources. Building the whole server is a heavyweight compile, so most readers should install a packaged server and keep the clone open next to the debugger.

Once a server is up, the “first model” of an AI product is usually a feature or metadata table: one row per user interaction, columns for the prompt, the model version, latency, and the outcome label. Standard SQL does the rest — inserts from your service, indexes for the access patterns, and transactions to keep counters and audit rows consistent. The value of the diagrams above is knowing what happens between that INSERT statement and the disk: a protocol packet becomes a parse tree, the optimizer compiles it into iterators, InnoDB inserts into a B-tree under a mini-transaction, and the redo log makes it durable before the client gets its OK.

The InnoDB Write Path: Mini-Transactions and the Redo Log

InnoDB’s unit of crash-safety is the mini-transaction. Every page modification — a row insert, a B-tree split, an undo record — is bracketed by an mtr that accumulates physical log records. When the mtr ends, mtr_t::commit, L577 publishes those records into the log buffer in one atomic step. From there a dedicated writer thread, log_writer_write_buffer, L2123, copies contiguous LSN ranges to the redo files. This is classic write-ahead logging: nothing dirty leaves the buffer pool before the redo that describes it is on disk.

The interplay shows up cleanly in the code. A full leaf page during insert triggers btr_page_split_and_insert, L2315, and the split’s structural changes ride the same mtr discipline as the row data. Meanwhile the page cleaner batches dirty pages with buf_flush_page_and_try_neighbors, L1394, which tries to flush adjacent pages in the same extent so one disk seek amortizes several writes. When memory pressure builds, eviction goes through buf_LRU_free_page, L956, which only frees a page whose redo is already durable. And a checkpointing thread — Log_checkpointing::log_checkpointer, L851 — advances the point from which crash recovery must replay, keeping restart time bounded no matter how far the write volume grows.

MVCC and Locking: Reading Without Blocking

The reason MySQL can serve dashboards and heavy writers from the same tables is multi-version concurrency. Every row carries hidden transaction columns, and a reader opens a snapshot: MVCC::view_open, L489 registers which transactions were active at snapshot time. As row_search_mvcc, L4437 walks an index, it consults that read view and reconstructs older row versions from undo records when a row has been modified after the snapshot began. A long-running analytical query therefore does not stall an insert-hungry ingestion service — the reader just sees the older, consistent world.

Writers, by contrast, use locks. lock_rec_lock, L1849 acquires record-level locks and queues waiters behind conflicting holders; if wait-for edges form a cycle, Deadlock_notifier::notify, L6054 walks the cycle, picks a victim, and rolls it back so the other transaction can proceed. Commit itself ends in trx_commit, L2293, which writes the commit record to redo and releases the locks. Understanding the split — MVCC for readers, locks for writers — explains most MySQL tuning advice you will ever read about isolation levels and gap locking.

The Optimizer and the Iterator Executor

Modern MySQL no longer interprets a parse tree directly. The optimizer’s plan — access paths — is compiled into a composition of row iterators. Leaf iterators such as TableScanIterator::DoRead, L276 wrap the handler calls, while composite iterators like AggregateIterator::DoRead, L290 implement grouping, joins, and materialization by pulling from children. This pull-based design is why EXPLAIN output maps so cleanly onto runtime behavior, and it is the piece to study if you are porting a query layer or benchmarking access patterns for an AI feature store.

Binlog Group Commit and Replication

Durability of a transaction has two halves: the engine’s redo log and the server’s binary log. The two-phase commit coordinator ha_commit_trans, L1686 hands the transaction to the binlog as a TC log via MYSQL_BIN_LOG::commit, L6807. The heart of throughput is MYSQL_BIN_LOG::ordered_commit, L7530: transactions are queued into flush, sync, and commit stages, with change_stage, L7278 serializing each stage so many concurrent writers amortize one fsync. That group commit behavior is why write-heavy AI event logging survives on commodity disks.

Replication is the natural extension: a dump thread running Binlog_sender::run, L386 streams events to each replica, where handle_slave_io, L5439 lands them in a relay log and handle_slave_sql, L7123 applies them. For read-heavy AI dashboards, replicas give you a scale-out read tier; for change-data-capture, the binlog is the feed you tap into with connectors that forward mutations to Kafka or a warehouse.

Honest Limits

  • The README is a pointer, not a manual. It contains no quick-start commands, no build recipes, and no performance claims — just downloads and docs links plus a license note. Everything operational lives at dev.mysql.com, not in the repo.
  • You are reading a moving target. The tree’s MYSQL_VERSION says 26.10.0-INNOVATION after LTS 9.7.0. Innovation releases move fast and carry newer, less battle-tested features; pin a packaged LTS for anything production-facing.
  • Source builds are heavy. The tracked tree is on the order of 61,000 files, and a from-scratch server build is a long CMake compile with sizeable dependencies — fine for study, not a quick afternoon.
  • No vector search out of the box. Unlike some Postgres extensions, MySQL has no native similarity-search index for embeddings; you pair it with a dedicated vector store or use application-level matching, which changes the architecture of embedding-driven features.
  • Replication lag is real. The async dump-and-apply design shown above means replicas trail the source; reading your own writes from a replica after an insert needs application care or semi-sync configurations.

MySQL rewards the time you spend in its source. The next time a feature store query or a replication hiccup puzzles you, the diagrams above give you a map, and the line-anchored links drop you straight into the exact function where the behavior lives.

entry.title: Neo4j Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Graph Database Engine

link.title: Neo4j Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Graph Database Engine

entry.content:
Every large language model application eventually hits the same wall: text alone cannot answer “how is entity A related to entity B through three intermediaries?” Vector search gives you semantic neighbors, but relationships — who funded whom, which user reviewed which order shipped to which address — live in edges, not embeddings. That is why knowledge graphs have become a standard backbone for RAG systems: an LLM extracts entities and relationships from raw text, writes them as graph nodes and edges, and retrieval then walks those edges across multiple hops with sub-second latency. Fraud rings, recommendation paths, bill-of-materials explosions, and drug-interaction chains all collapse into the same shape problem.

Neo4j is the most widely deployed native graph database, and its GitHub repository hosts the full Community Edition source in Java. Native is the operative word: unlike a relational engine that would answer a three-hop traversal with repeated joins, Neo4j stores relationships as physical pointers between records, so each hop is one dereference instead of a scan. For multi-hop queries this is the difference between milliseconds and minutes, and it is exactly the access pattern GraphRAG-style retrievers generate in volume. If your stack already leans on vector stores like Milvus or Qdrant for semantic recall, a graph store complements them by answering the structural questions embeddings cannot.

This post is a source tour of that engine. We compiled two architecture diagrams from the current 2026.10 branch and verified every class and line number below directly in the tree. The first diagram shows the end-to-end life of a query; the second zooms into the classes that do the work.

The request path at a glance: a Bolt driver connection is parsed, planned, and executed against the kernel transaction API, which buffers changes in TxState and commits them through the record storage engine, the page cache, and the write-ahead log.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BoltProtocol, L66 is the interface every wire-protocol version implements; handshake classes like ModernProtocolHandshakeHandler, L35 negotiate which of the versioned handlers (v40 through v61) will decode the session.
  • StateMachineImpl, L41 is the connection state machine that walks a session through READY, STREAMING, and transaction states, rejecting out-of-order messages as protocol errors.
  • Cypher5AstParser, L39 turns query text into an AST; CachingPreParser, L79 normalizes queries first and serves repeated statements from a cache.
  • IDPQueryGraphSolver, L144 is the cost-based planner core, using iterative dynamic programming over join orders, with CardinalityCostModel, L160 scoring each candidate.
  • CypherRuntime, L55 binds a plan to an execution engine; InterpretedRuntime, L72 compiles the plan into a tree of operators such as AllNodesScanPipe, L28 and ProduceResultsPipe, L31.
  • KernelTransactionImplementation, L210 is the transaction workhorse: its commit at L1195 funnels into commitTransaction at L1325, which hands the buffered TxState, L110 to the commit process.
  • BatchingTransactionAppender, L35 serializes the command batch and its appendToLog at L107 writes it through EnvelopedWALService, L35, the enveloped write-ahead log.
  • RecordStorageEngine, L146 applies the commands via apply at L511; NeoStores, L60 owns the individual stores, all reading and writing through the PageCache, L47.

The detail view: each block is a real class in the repository — click any node in the source diagram to open the file at the exact line cited here.

Bolt: The Wire Protocol Under Every Driver

Every official driver — Python, JavaScript, Java, Go — speaks Bolt, a compact binary protocol over a single TCP connection. The server side lives in community/bolt. Negotiation is layered: the handshake handler reads the client’s proposed versions, the registry resolves them to a concrete BoltProtocol implementation, and that implementation constructs the state machine and message processors for the session. The design pays off for AI agents that hold long sessions: one multiplexed connection carries many queries, and the FSM keeps a slow streaming result from blocking a new query.

Cypher: Parsing and the IDP Cost Planner

Cypher is Neo4j’s declarative graph query language — pattern matching rather than table joins. Compilation happens in stages: the pre-parser normalizes and caches, the ANTLR-based parser builds the AST, semantic analysis decorates it, and the logical planner converts patterns into plan operators. The interesting part is join ordering: the IDP solver builds larger plan fragments from the cheapest combinations of smaller ones, guided by the cardinality model that estimates how many rows each pattern will match. Graph statistics — labels, relationship types, selectivity — feed those estimates, which is why freshly loaded graphs sometimes plan poorly until statistics accumulate. The interpreted runtime then lowers the plan into a pipe tree, each pipe pulling rows from its source, with cursors into the kernel underneath.

The Kernel: TxState and the Commit Path

The kernel is the ACID heart. A transaction is a KernelTransactionImplementation instance with a TxState object that buffers every mutation — reads see committed data plus their own writes through an overlay. On commit, three things happen in a strict order: changes are converted into a storage-agnostic command batch, that batch is appended to the write-ahead log, and only then is it applied to the stores. The CommandBatch interface at L30 is the contract between kernel and storage engine, which is why the same kernel can drive different storage backends. The WAL itself was recently carved into its own community/wal module; the enveloped format wraps each entry with a header and checksum so torn writes at the tail of a crash are detected and truncated cleanly at recovery.

Record Storage: Index-Free Adjacency on Disk

The record storage engine implements the kernel contract with fixed-size records. NodeStore keeps one record per node — flags, first relationship pointer, first property pointer. RelationshipStore is the clever bit: each relationship record stores both endpoints plus prev/next pointers per direction, so a node’s relationships form doubly linked lists threaded through the relationship file. Traversing from node A to node B means reading A’s record, chasing one pointer to a relationship record, and dereferencing the other endpoint — no index lookup, no join. Properties live in PropertyStore blocks with small values inlined and large ones spilling into DynamicRecord chains. Every store file is mapped through the Muninn page cache, a fork of the design used by the engine itself for the StorageReader, L42 cursors the runtime consumes, and the record format — standard or page-aligned — is selected at store creation by RecordFormatSelector, L62. Compared to the B-tree workhorses behind PostgreSQL or the single-file simplicity of SQLite, this is a storage layout only a graph can love: pointer chasing instead of key lookups. Secondary indexes — native GBPTree range indexes from RangeIndexProvider, L104 and Lucene-backed text indexes — accelerate entry points, but the traversal itself stays pointer-driven.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository builds like most large Java projects, and the README keeps it honest about the prerequisites. You need Apache Maven 3.9.11 or newer plus a supported JDK — the README suggests openjdk-21-jdk on Ubuntu — and Maven itself needs extra heap: export MAVEN_OPTS="-Xmx2048m". With those in place, a plain mvn clean install -T1C builds the individual jars with tests; if you only want the artifacts, the README recommends mvn clean install -DskipTests -T1C. After the build completes, cd into packaging/standalone/target, extract the distribution you want, and run the server start script. From a knowledge-graph angle, the fastest way to a first model is to feed extracted triples — subject, predicate, object — through the official Python driver with MERGE statements so re-runs deduplicate nodes and edges, then attach your embeddings as node properties where you want hybrid retrieval. Give the page cache a meaningful share of RAM in neo4j.conf before loading real data; a graph that fits in cache is a different animal from one that thrashes.

Honest Limits

  • Community versus Enterprise. The README is explicit: Community Edition is GPLv3, while Enterprise includes closed-source components that are not in this repository. Practical consequences: online backup, hot resizing, and the clustering and causal-read replication stack are Enterprise features, so this repo’s Community server is effectively single-node.
  • Repository layout. The public tree contains the community/ modules, annotations, and packaging — there is no enterprise/ source here, so any tour of replication or multi-database cluster internals will hit a closed door in the public code.
  • JVM memory tuning. This is a Java engine with two memory pools to budget — heap for execution and transaction state, page cache for the store files. The build itself asks for 2 GB of Maven heap, and undersized production heaps show up as GC pauses, not clean errors.
  • Cypher ecosystem maturity. Cypher is expressive for patterns, but the broader tooling — BI connectors, ORMs, migration frameworks — is thinner than the SQL ecosystem around PostgreSQL; property-graph extensions exist for relational engines, but they do not match a native engine’s traversal performance.
  • GPLv3 obligations. GPLv3 is viral in a way MIT and Apache licenses are not; if you distribute a product containing Community Edition, the license terms follow it.

Where does Neo4j sit in a modern retrieval stack? Treat it as the structural half: the entity-relationship skeleton your extraction step writes to, queried with Cypher to assemble multi-hop context for the model before generation. Vector stores answer the semantic half — neighbors in embedding space, with the schema-free flexibility that makes them quick to bootstrap — and the two compose into hybrid retrieval that neither approach provides alone. The storage philosophies are also worth contrasting: where log-structured engines continuously rewrite the disk layout to make writes fast, Neo4j’s fixed records and stable pointers make reads and traversals predictable, and that choice is visible everywhere in the source you just toured — two very different answers to the same question of what a database engine should spend its I/O budget on.
