entry.title: PostgreSQL Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Engine Powering Your AI Data Layer

link.title: PostgreSQL Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Engine Powering Your AI Data Layer

entry.content:
Ask around any serious ML team and you will hear the same answer to the question “where does your data actually live?”: PostgreSQL. The vector search boom did not replace it — it extended it, with pgvector and friends turning a battle-tested relational engine into the metadata store, embedding index, and retrieval backend for retrieval-augmented generation systems. Search layers such as ParadeDB are built directly on top of Postgres, feature stores use it as their source of truth, and experiment-tracking servers default to it as their persistence layer. The default is not nostalgia: it is the consequence of thirty years of correctness work on transactions, concurrency, and recovery.

What makes that trust interesting is that PostgreSQL is written in C, in the open, in a codebase that has been continuously developed since the 1980s. Nothing in it is hidden behind a vendor wall. When you call SELECT from a client, a forked operating-system process walks your SQL through a real compiler front end, a cost-based optimizer, a tuple-at-a-time executor, a shared buffer pool, and a write-ahead log before anything touches disk. Understanding that path changes how you tune it — why a naive UPDATE-heavy feature table bloats, why connections are expensive, why a checkpoint can cause a latency spike.

This post is a source tour of the postgres/postgres mirror on the master branch. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams were generated from the same checkout. We follow one query from the wire to the WAL, then step inside the planner, MVCC visibility, recovery, and the maintenance machinery that keeps it all honest. The goal is not to make you a PostgreSQL hacker in one sitting — it is to give you a map accurate enough that when something misbehaves in production, you know which corner of the source to open first.

The life of a query: one client connection, one forked backend, one pass through the SQL compilers, executor, buffer manager, and write-ahead log.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The client never talks to storage. Applications link against libpq, and the connection is established by PQconnectdb, L825, which resolves the conninfo string and runs the startup handshake.
  • One process per connection. The postmaster binds the listen sockets in PostmasterMain, L496 and forks a dedicated backend per client via BackendStartup, L3599 — isolation by process boundary, not threads.
  • The session loop. Each backend lives in exec_simple_query, L1030, the per-statement cycle that parses, plans, executes, and formats results for every string the client sends.
  • Parsing is two stages. raw_parser, L42 turns SQL text into raw parse trees, and transformTopLevelStmt, L265 resolves names and types into a semantically checked Query.
  • Views and policies happen here. The rewriter’s QueryRewrite, L4649 expands views, applies rules, and enforces row security before any cost model sees the query.
  • The optimizer is a search. standard_planner, L357 drives it: make_one_rel, L183 builds access paths per relation, and make_join_rel, L746 enumerates join orders and methods.
  • Execution is a pull chain. ExecutorRun, L308 starts the plan, and nodes like ExecHashJoin, L818 pull tuples upward one at a time.
  • Every change is logged first. Writes go through the heap in heap_insert, L2007 and become durable via XLogInsert, L486 — the record reaches the WAL before the page itself is dirty.

Inside the machine: the optimizer's join search, the executor's node zoo, the buffer pool internals, MVCC visibility, and the background processes for checkpoints and vacuum.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps it deliberately short: get the software from postgresql.org/download, and read the installation documentation for the build from source. Building from the tree confirms why. The Makefile refuses to do anything until you have configured the tree — run ./configure, and only then do the GNU make targets make, make check, and make install become meaningful (the top-level Makefile even prints “You need to run the ‘configure’ program first” if you skip it, and it insists on GNU make specifically). make check runs the regression suite that has guarded executor and planner behavior for decades.

Once installed, the tree’s own tools bootstrap a cluster: initdb (its source lives at src/bin/initdb/initdb.c) creates the data directory, createdb (src/bin/scripts/createdb.c) makes your database, and the interactive terminal psql (src/bin/psql/) connects you. Your first query — a CREATE TABLE for model metadata, a few INSERTs of experiment runs, a SELECT with a join — exercises exactly the path in the overview diagram. For ML use, that first table is often the seed of a feature store: an immutable-events table plus a materialized current-state table, both served by the same engine your notebook already connects to through libpq.

Inside the Planner

PostgreSQL’s optimizer is not a rule engine; it is an explicit search over paths. make_one_rel walks every base relation and produces the candidate access paths — sequential scans, index scans, and their parameterized variants — each annotated with estimated startup and total costs. When a join is possible, make_join_rel considers each join order and method, prunes by cost, and keeps only the cheapest path per relation set. Only after the search converges does create_plan translate the winning Path tree into the Plan nodes the executor actually runs.

The practical consequence for analytics-adjacent ML work is that plan quality is an estimation problem. The planner trusts its statistics; stale statistics after a bulk load of training data can flip a hash join into a nested loop. The standard defense is operational, not architectural: analyze after large loads, and read EXPLAIN before complaining about speed.

MVCC and the Real Cost of an UPDATE

PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place. An update inserts a new tuple version and marks the old one dead-for-everyone-eventually. Visibility is decided by HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC in src/backend/access/heap/heapam_visibility.c (L939), which inspects the inserting and deleting transaction IDs of each candidate tuple against the reader’s snapshot. Commit status comes from the CLOG, where TransactionIdSetStatusBit (L131) packs four states per transaction into shared bitmaps that every backend consults.

This design is why readers never block writers and writers never block readers — a large property for serving features while backfills run. The price is paid in dead tuples. A feature table updated on every training run accumulates versions that only VACUUM can reclaim; heap_vacuum_rel in src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c (L624) does that scavenging, and the autovacuum launcher (AutoVacWorkerMain, L1413) triggers it by thresholds you can tune per table. Append-only event tables and periodically rebuilt aggregates are the idiomatic way to keep that machinery bored.

WAL: How a Commit Survives a Crash

Durability in PostgreSQL has a strict order: log first, page later. Before a backend modifies any shared page, it assembles a record via XLogInsert and writes it to the WAL buffers; the commit record’s flush is what a returning COMMIT actually waits for. Checkpoints, run by the dedicated checkpointer process (CheckpointerMain, L206) and implemented around CreateCheckPoint in src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c (L7692), force all dirty buffers to disk and write a marker so that recovery never has to replay from the beginning of time.

At startup after a crash, StartupXLOG (L6083, same file) locates the last valid checkpoint and the recovery machinery replays forward, with ApplyWalRecord in src/backend/access/transam/xlogrecovery.c (L1906) re-applying each record’s changes to the pages. The whole scheme means a lost machine loses nothing acknowledged, and it is also the foundation of physical replication — which is how most teams give their metadata store a hot standby.

Where PostgreSQL Fits in an AI Stack

The engine’s role in ML infrastructure is usually “system of record plus retrieval.” With pgvector, embeddings live beside the features they describe, and the planner’s index choices matter as much for ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT 10 as for any join. For hybrid lexical-plus-semantic search, ParadeDB adds BM25 scoring and analytics inside Postgres itself rather than exporting data to a separate cluster. For heavy feature computations, a common shape pairs Postgres with DuckDB: transactional truth in Postgres, columnar scanning and vectorized aggregation outside it. A Redis tier in front absorbs hot-path lookups, and if your events are really time-series, QuestDB-style stores can own the high-ingest tail while Postgres keeps the relational core. The point of the diagrams above is that whichever extension you bolt on, it enters through the same parser, planner, and executor everyone else uses — and that is also why extension quality varies so widely. An extension that mishandles the buffer pinning or snapshot rules the core enforces can corrupt state in ways the core cannot see. Prefer extensions that ship in reputable distributions, pin their versions in your infrastructure code, and test them against your real query mix, because the C ABI they ride on is stable but not forgiving.

Honest Limits

Read the source and the trade-offs are visible rather than hidden. First, the process-per-connection model that BackendStartup implements is robust but heavy: thousands of client connections mean thousands of processes, which is why external poolers are near-mandatory at scale. Second, MVCC’s copy-on-write means unvacuumed bloat is a real failure mode, and autovacuum defaults are tuned conservatively — write-heavy tables need attention. Third, the executor pulls tuples one at a time through virtual function calls; this is superb for transactional access and merely adequate for scanning billions of rows, which is why columnar systems and analytical engines exist alongside rather than instead of Postgres. Fourth, planning is only as good as its statistics — the optimizer will confidently misestimate on skewed data. None of these are bugs; they are the design’s edges, and knowing where they are is what separates operating Postgres from merely installing it.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the PostgreSQL C source — from libpq and the postmaster to the planner, the MVCC heap, and the write-ahead log — with architecture diagrams that show how the world's most trusted open-source database really runs.

entry.title: RocksDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Storage Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure

link.title: RocksDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the LSM Storage Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure

entry.content:
RocksDB is the storage engine you have probably used today without noticing. It sits underneath Flink’s checkpointed operator state, Kafka Streams’ local state stores, TiKV (the transactional key-value layer that powers TiDB), and a growing family of feature stores that keep precomputed ML features close to model servers. Wherever a system must persist fast-changing state on a single node — high-frequency telemetry ingestion, embeddings stored by key, feature rows joined at inference time — an embedded engine that absorbs writes quickly is the difference between a flat tail-latency graph and a wall of write stalls.

That engine is almost always an LSM tree, not a B-tree. Classical relational engines organize data with B-trees: PostgreSQL’s heap plus B-tree indexes and InnoDB’s clustered index inside MySQL both mutate pages in place, which is excellent for reads but turns every random insert into several page writes. We walked both designs in our PostgreSQL and MySQL server source tours, and SQLite applies the same in-place philosophy to its b-tree layer. An LSM inverts the trade: it accepts writes into an in-memory structure, appends a recovery log for durability, and rewrites data later in bulk sequential passes. For machine-learning workloads — heavy feature updates, training-event ingestion, state written far more often than read — that inversion is exactly what you want.

Here we read facebook/rocksdb at its main branch and trace the lifecycle of one key: from DB::Put through the write-ahead log, the skip-list memtable, a flush into an SST file, background compaction, and the read path that stitches all layers back together. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams link each node to its source file.

RocksDB at a glance: the write path flows left to right through WAL and memtable into L0 files, while background threads rewrite data downward and every change is published through the manifest-backed VersionSet.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Write admission. DBImpl::Write, L230 is the front door for all mutations; it funnels every writer into WriteImpl, where concurrent writers are grouped under a single leader.
  • Durability first. Writer::AddRecord, L87 frames each batch as a CRC32C-checksummed record in the write-ahead log before anything becomes visible.
  • In-memory ingest. MemTable::Add, L1132 encodes sequence number, type, key, and value into an arena-allocated entry of the active memtable.
  • Flush trigger. FlushJob::Run, L224 streams an immutable memtable into a fresh L0 SST file on the flush thread.
  • SST construction. BlockBasedTableBuilder::Add, L2209 packs entries into compressed data blocks while the builder accumulates index and filter blocks for the final file.
  • Background rewrites. CompactionJob::Run, L1282 merges overlapping runs into lower levels, discarding shadowed and deleted data.
  • Metadata publication. VersionSet::LogAndApply, L6641 is the single serialized point where new file lists are appended to the MANIFEST and swapped in as an immutable Version.
  • Reads. DBImpl::GetImpl, L155 checks live and immutable memtables first, then probes the current Version’s levels newest-first.

The detailed view expands each stage into its concrete functions: leader/follower write batching, the InlineSkipList, BuildTable, bloom filters inside the block-based table format, and the compaction iterator that resolves duplicates and merge operands.

Why a Write-Optimized Engine Matters for ML Workloads

The clearest evidence for the LSM design is who embeds it. Flink offers a RocksDB-backed state backend precisely because windowed aggregations and join buffers update state thousands of times per second, far more than they scan it. Kafka Streams ships RocksDB as its default local store for the same reason. TiKV layered the Raft-replicated transactional protocol on top, and vector-search extensions treat it as a durable index substrate. In each case the pattern repeats: an analytics or serving system needs a per-node, crash-safe, write-heavy cache that survives restarts without the ceremony of running a database server.

The recovery story matters as much as the speed. Because every mutation lands in both the WAL and the memtable, a job that crashes mid-window restarts with its state intact: the engine replays the log, rebuilds the memtable, and serving continues. That property — durable local state without a network round trip per update — is what let stream processors move window aggregation off remote databases. It also reshapes the failure modes: instead of lock contention you watch for write stalls, L0 pileups, and compaction debt, all of which are visible in this source tree rather than hidden behind a query planner.

RocksDB’s answer is to make the expensive work asynchronous. A put pays for one log append plus one in-memory insert, and the reorganization cost is deferred to background threads that batch many updates into sequential file rewrites. That is also why it behaves so differently from a general SQL engine: it deliberately accumulates redundancy across levels and cleans it up later, a bet that wins when writes dominate.

The LSM Idea, in Code

The write path shows the design’s economy. Inside WriteImpl, writers queue up and WriteThread::EnterAsMemTableWriter, L574 elects one leader that will write the WAL and install memtable entries on behalf of the whole group — turning N concurrent writers into one sequential append. DBImpl::WriteToWAL, L2330 merges the group into a single batch. Once the record is durable, WriteBatchInternal::InsertInto, L3296 replays the serialized batch, and the MemTableInserter, L2045 handler translates each Put/Delete/Merge record into memtable calls.

The memtable itself is a probabilistic skip list rather than a balanced tree. SkipListRep::Insert, L42 forwards into InlineSkipList::Insert, L103, a lock-free structure where concurrent inserts and reads never block each other — one reason RocksDB can saturate multi-core writers without latching the memtable. Because the list is kept sorted, the later flush is a simple merge pass, not a re-sort.

Flush and the SST File Format

When the active memtable fills, the flush thread takes over. DBImpl::BackgroundCallFlush, L4999 loops forever picking work, and MemTableList::PickMemtablesToFlush, L495 selects the oldest immutable memtables. DBImpl::FlushMemTableToOutputFile, L191 builds the job, and BuildTable, L74 — shared with compaction — turns an iterator stream into one sorted file.

The file format is where reads stay fast. BlockBasedTableBuilder::Finish, L4018 emits the index blocks, metadata, and footer after the data blocks are written. Alongside, FullFilterBlockBuilder::Add, L67 accumulates bloom/Ribbon bits for every key prefix, so a point lookup can reject a whole file with one hash probe. On the read side, BlockBasedTable::Open, L738 loads footer and index into memory, and the per-SST lookup defined in BlockBasedTable::Get, L509 consults the filter before fetching a single data block.

Compaction: Paying Down Write Debt

Compaction is the LSM’s garbage collector. DBImpl::BackgroundCallCompaction, L5100 drives the loop, and LevelCompactionPicker::PickCompaction, L1000 chooses a level plus overlapping inputs using score-based heuristics. CompactionJob::Run, L1282 then merges those runs through CompactionIterator::NextFromInput, L1012, the heart of the engine: it deduplicates sequence numbers, respects snapshots, drops tombstones once they reach the bottom level, and applies compaction filters. User-defined merges are resolved by MergeHelper::MergeUntil, L281 using whatever MergeOperator the application supplied.

Every rewrite ends at VersionSet::LogAndApply, L6641 — flushes and compactions both publish through it, which is why readers never see a half-installed file list. Applications can also force the process with DB::CompactRange at DBImpl::CompactRange, L1192, useful before long-lived range scans or after bulk loads.

Leveled is only the default style. The same directory carries a universal picker for write-heavy workloads that prefer many small overlapping runs, and a FIFO picker that simply drops data once a size or TTL threshold passes — compaction_picker_universal.cc and compaction_picker_fifo.cc sit beside compaction_picker_level.cc in the tree. All of them feed the same CompactionJob machinery, so a column family can switch styles through options without touching the rest of the engine.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository’s INSTALL.md keeps the build deliberately simple. The library compiles with C++20 and needs GCC 11 or newer (or Clang 10 or newer) per INSTALL.md L9. The recommended target is make static_lib, producing librocksdb.a in release mode (INSTALL.md L13); make shared_lib builds the shared variant instead. If the binary must run on older CPUs, set PORTABLE=1 (INSTALL.md L25). Compression libraries — zlib, bzip2, lz4, snappy, zstandard — are optional link-time accelerators (INSTALL.md L35), and only the tools need gflags; the library builds without it.

Your first program is thirty lines. The public surface starts at DB::Open, L289, and examples/simple_example.cc shows the canonical skeleton: open at DB::Open(options, kDBPath, &db), L38, then write at db->Put, L42. To turn this into a feature-store skeleton, define a column family per feature group via ColumnFamilyOptions, batch feature-row upserts into one WriteBatch per inference request, and set bloom filters on — the filter block you saw in the format section is what keeps point lookups at a handful of comparisons.

Honest Limits

  • It is a library, not a database. The README states plainly that “this code is a library that forms the core building block for a fast key-value server” (README.md L7). There is no SQL layer, no network protocol, and no replication scheme included — systems like TiKV build those on top.
  • Read amplification is real. The project itself advertises tradeoffs between write-, read-, and space-amplification factors (README.md L9). A cold Get may probe the memtable, immutable memtables, and one file per level; the bloom filter bounds, but does not eliminate, that cost.
  • Tuning is a discipline. DBOptions and ColumnFamilyOptions in options.h L601 expose hundreds of knobs, and the repository carries a DEFAULT_OPTIONS_HISTORY.md to track how defaults changed across releases — a hint about how much behavior depends on them.
  • Build defaults can mislead. INSTALL.md warns in its first lines that plain make compiles debug-mode binaries that are “much slower than release mode” (INSTALL.md L3); benchmarks built from default targets will undersell the engine.

An LSM engine is a wager that the future rewrites what you wrote yesterday. RocksDB implements that wager with unusual rigor — a lock-free memtable, crash-safe group commit, immutable SSTs, and a versioned manifest — which is why so much of the AI infrastructure stack, from stream processors to feature stores, keeps choosing it as the last write stop before disk.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of facebook/rocksdb, the LSM-tree storage engine embedded in TiKV, Flink, and Kafka Streams, tracing the write path, skip-list memtable, SST files, and background compaction through verified code anchors.

entry.title: SQLite Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the World’s Most Deployed Database

link.title: SQLite Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the World’s Most Deployed Database

entry.content:
SQLite is almost certainly running within arm’s reach of you right now. It is the database inside every phone, every major browser, most operating systems, and an enormous share of embedded devices. It has no server process, no network protocol, and no configuration file — it is a C library that links into your application and owns a single file on disk. That design is exactly why the AI world keeps adopting it: edge inference boxes, local-first desktop apps, and on-device retrieval all need structured state without operating a database cluster.

The AI connection has become concrete. Embedding-heavy applications increasingly treat SQLite as a local vector store — the popular sqlite-vec extension follows in the footsteps of the in-tree vec1 ANN extension that now lives in ext/vec1/, and full-text retrieval has shipped in the core tree for years as FTS5. When you build on-device RAG, an agent’s memory store, or a local-first annotation layer for model outputs, you are deploying this codebase. Understanding its internals therefore pays off in the same way our tours of (PostgreSQL) and (MySQL) did: the storage layer you depend on stops being a black box.

In this tour we read the sqlite/sqlite GitHub mirror of the canonical Fossil repository (version 3.55.0 at the time of writing). Two diagrams anchor the walk: a compact overview of the layer stack, and a detailed graph of the compile path and the write path with real function names and line numbers.

Layer view of SQLite. Statements enter through the public API, are compiled to a VDBE program, and execute down through B-tree, pager, and WAL into the pluggable VFS.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Client entry — sqlite3_exec, L30 is the classic one-shot helper: it prepares each statement and steps it to completion. Connections themselves are created by sqlite3_open_v2, L3768, which allocates the handle and attaches one B-tree per database file.
  • Compile — sqlite3_prepare_v2, L972 compiles one SQL string into a virtual-machine program.
  • Tokenize — sqlite3RunParser, L600 walks the text, classifies tokens, and drives the parser.
  • Grammar — sqlite3Parser, L59 is a Lemon LALR(1) grammar, not hand-written C; tool/lemon.c generates parse.c from it at build time.
  • Plan and emit — sqlite3WhereBegin, L6954 is the query planner: it picks indexes and join orders and emits the loop opcodes.
  • Execute — sqlite3VdbeExec, L903 is the register-based virtual machine — one giant switch over opcodes.
  • Store — sqlite3BtreeBeginTrans, L3838 opens transactions on the B-tree, and sqlite3PagerSharedLock, L5323 is where journaling and locking begin.
  • Durability — in WAL mode the pager hands frames to sqlite3WalFrames, L4376; everything ultimately lands on disk through the VFS, e.g. unixRead, L3512.

Detailed graph: the compile path from tokens to opcodes on top, the storage stack from B-tree cells to VFS writes below, with the WAL branch on the side.

From Install to Your First Model

Building SQLite from this repository is deliberately boring — that is part of its engineering culture. On Unix, the README prescribes: install gcc make tcl-dev, unpack the tree, create a build directory, then run ../sqlite/configure followed by make sqlite3 for the command-line shell and make sqlite3.c for the amalgamation. Core deliverables build without TCL; TCL is only needed for the test targets. On Windows the tree ships a make.bat so make sqlite3.exe works under MSVC, or you can call nmake /f Makefile.msc directly.

The amalgamation deserves a moment. make sqlite3.c runs Tcl scripts that stitch every source and header into one enormous translation unit — over 200K lines. Compile-time cross-procedure analysis across that single file makes the engine about 5% faster than building from separate objects, which is why every language binding embeds the amalgamation rather than the tree.

Now your “first model” — in the AI sense, a table of embeddings. The tree contains ext/vec1/vec1.c, an ANN vector extension (version 0.8) whose header documents an AVX2 loadable build: gcc -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx2 -mfma vec1.c -shared -fPIC -o vec1.so. Load it through the standard extension entry sqlite3_extension_init, L13145; it exposes L2 and cosine distance metrics (constants at L26) and reports itself with SELECT vec1_info(). For keyword recall, FTS5 ships in-tree and initializes via sqlite3Fts5Init, L3906. A hybrid store — FTS5 for lexical, vec1 for dense, plus your own metadata columns — fits comfortably in one file, which is precisely the local-RAG shape many apps want before graduating to a dedicated server like (Qdrant).

The Compile Path: SQL Text to a VM Program

Compilation starts in sqlite3Prepare, L717, a driver that resolves schemas and retries if the schema version changes underneath it. It hands the SQL text to sqlite3RunParser, L600, whose inner loop calls a token classifier and then the Lemon-generated parser. The grammar file src/parse.y carries the %name sqlite3Parser directive; each grammar action either builds AST objects (Expr, Select, Table) or calls code generators directly.

DDL flows through sqlite3StartTable, L1292, which allocates the Table object and root pages, and sqlite3EndTable, L2757, which writes the schema row and emits OP_ParseSchema. Queries flow through sqlite3Select, L7807, the top-level SELECT compiler. Expressions funnel into sqlite3ExprCodeTarget, L5110, which turns an expression tree into opcodes that leave results in registers. The planner call from select.c is sqlite3WhereBegin, L6954; when it returns, the join loops are coded, and sqlite3WhereEnd, L7657 closes them and frees the plan. Every emitted instruction lands through sqlite3VdbeAddOp3, L274, and sqlite3VdbeMakeReady, L2664 finalizes the program frame.

Inside the VDBE

SQLite’s execution model is a bytecode interpreter, not a tree-walker — a choice that gives it deterministic, steppable execution: sqlite3_step() runs the program until the next row is ready. The public stepping entry is sqlite3_step, L990, and the interpreter core is sqlite3VdbeExec, L903. Even the opcode list itself is generated: a Tcl script scans src/vdbe.c to produce opcodes.h and opcodes.c (the README documents this). When a statement finishes, sqlite3VdbeHalt, L3348 decides whether to commit, roll back, or just release cursors. EXPLAIN simply prints this program, so every statement you run has a fully visible assembly listing — an excellent debugging surface for AI agents that generate SQL at runtime.

The Storage Stack: B-Tree, Pager, WAL

Below the VM sits the classic three-layer stack. The B-tree layer (sqlite3BtreeOpen, L2565) manages pages, cursors, and balancing: sqlite3BtreeCursor, L4802 positions a cursor, accessPayload, L5158 decodes record bytes including overflow pages, and sqlite3BtreeInsert, L9445 writes cells and rebalances. Transactions open at sqlite3BtreeBeginTrans, L3838 and commit at sqlite3BtreeCommit, L4467.

The pager (sqlite3PagerSharedLock, L5323) owns locking, journaling, and the page cache. Page fetches enter at sqlite3PagerGet, L5795 (its worker getPageNormal at L5604 resolves reads from the WAL when needed). Commits split into two phases — sqlite3PagerCommitPhaseOne, L6534 and sqlite3PagerCommitPhaseTwo, L6771 — and choose a durability route: the rollback-journal path journals pages first and rewrites them through pager_write_pagelist, L4490, while the WAL path appends frames instead (the call site for sqlite3WalFrames sits at pager.c:3280).

The WAL branch is worth studying on its own. After a crash, walIndexRecover, L1422 rebuilds the wal-index from the log; readers binary-search it with sqlite3WalFindFrame, L3737 and copy page images via sqlite3WalReadFrame, L3755; writers serialize through the write lock at sqlite3WalBeginWriteTransaction, L3800. Because every I/O goes through the pluggable VFS dispatch (sqlite3OsWrite, L92 into unixWrite, L3643), the whole engine ports to exotic filesystems by implementing one small interface — the same trick that lets the vector and FTS extensions live in one file with your metadata.

SQLite in the AI Data Layer

Why should an AI engineer care? Because the modern stack keeps rediscovering that most intelligence workloads start small and local. Prototypes store embeddings next to the app that computes them; agents keep session state and tool results in a file; edge devices log inferences where the network is not guaranteed. SQLite’s zero-administration design means the “database deployment” is a linked library and a filename. Compared with embedded analytical engines like (DuckDB) — which we tour separately — SQLite optimizes for transactional durability and tiny footprint rather than columnar scans, and the two compose well in the same process. And when a local store outgrows one machine, the migration path to server systems like (Qdrant) for vectors or (PostgreSQL) for general workloads is straightforward because the data model is plain SQL. Allocation is centralized too: everything from VM registers to page-cache frames flows through sqlite3_malloc64, L322, so memory profiling a local RAG service has a single choke point. Even authorization is pluggable at the compile step via sqlite3_set_authorizer, L70, which multi-tenant tooling can use to gate which statements an LLM is allowed to run.

Honest Limits

SQLite is not a client/server database, and the source makes that unmistakable: there is no network listener anywhere in the tree — the “client” is a function call and the storage backends are file VFS implementations. Concurrency is bounded: WAL mode permits one writer at a time, enforced by the single WAL write lock, and cross-process coordination relies on file locking rather than a broker. There are no server-side user accounts; access control is whatever the host process enforces through the authorizer callback. The engine also carries real complexity — the README itself warns that the amalgamation exceeds 200K lines, chokes some symbolic debuggers, and that it “will not be the easiest library in the world to hack.” None of this diminishes its role; it defines it. For the AI data layer, SQLite is the floor of the pyramid — the substrate on which (MySQL) and the server engines above it were eventually needed.
entry.summary: A source tour of the sqlite/sqlite repository showing how the tokenizer, Lemon parser, VDBE virtual machine, B-tree, pager, WAL, and VFS layers turn SQL text into durable pages.
